problems.stem: A design memo opens: "First I built the storyboard, then I ran a pilot, then I revised the feedback." Why does this fail as a design memo?
options: It is too short to count as a memo.
It recounts activity rather than arguing for a recommended decision the reader must act on.
It mentions a pilot, which does not belong in a memo.
Memos should never be written in the first person.
problems.explanation: A design memo makes an argument for a decision. A chronological activity log gives the reader nothing to decide.

problems.stem: A memo argues well but names no recipient and no decision. What does it most need?
options: More citations to course readings.
A named audience and the specific decision that audience owns (for example, the program lead deciding whether to fund the screen-reader build).
A longer background section.
A different font for the heading.
problems.explanation: A memo to no one, about no decision, cannot be acted on. Naming the audience and the decision they own makes it actionable.

problems.stem: Your memo recommends Tool A over Tool B. BigAL suggests strengthening it by adding your narration-timing finding from an earlier section, which you are proud of. What is the defensible move?
options: Accept it; more evidence always makes a memo more persuasive.
Reject it and document why: the narration-timing finding does not bear on the Tool A versus Tool B decision, so including it dilutes the argument.
Accept it but move it to an appendix so it is technically present.
Reject it because AI suggestions should never be used in a memo.
problems.explanation: Claim-to-evidence discipline means using only the evidence that bears on the decision. The accessibility gate and the pilot's low-vision result bear on the tool choice; the narration-timing finding, however good, does not. The bounded AI move is to reject the suggestion and record the reason, which is exactly the documented accept-and-reject trail the memo's AI-use note requires.

problems.stem: A memo recommends adopting Tool A and attaches pilot data and an audit matrix as appendices, but the body never references them. What is the strongest evidence-based revision?
options: Delete the appendices to shorten the memo.
Tie each evidence item to the claim it supports in the body (for example, cite the 3-of-5 pilot miss when arguing the accessibility gate), so the data becomes the argument rather than decoration.
Move the appendices to the front of the memo.
Add more appendices to look thorough.
problems.explanation: Unlinked evidence is decoration. Connecting each data point to the claim it backs turns attachments into the memo's actual argument.

problems.stem: Two teammates revise the same weak memo. One swaps in a cleaner template, tightens the prose, and adds a professional header. The other moves the recommendation to the first sentence and attaches the audit score and pilot result to the specific claims they support. Which revision is evidence-based, and why?
options: The first, because stakeholders judge memos by their presentation quality.
The second, because it changes how the reader can act on the argument: the recommendation is findable and each claim is now checkable against its evidence.
Both equally; any change made after feedback counts as evidence-based revision.
Neither; a memo can only be improved by collecting new pilot data.
problems.explanation: Polish changes how the memo looks; evidence-based revision changes how the argument works. Restructuring to BLUF and linking claims to their evidence are revisions a reviewer can trace to the memo's job as a decision instrument. The cleaner template is fine but does not address why the memo was failing.
